title: (Scenario) Design a real-time delivery tracking pipeline with Flink — Kafka source (partitioned by user_id) → map (enrich) → keyBy(user_id) → tumbling window (30 min) → aggregate stats → JDBC sink (PostgreSQL) — explaining parallelism, forwarding vs redistributing patterns, and fault tolerance via checkpoints.
shortTitle: Design a real-time delivery tracking pipeline with Flink

s1_definition.profdef: The pipeline is a Flink streaming job that ingests delivery events from a Kafka source partitioned by user id, enriches each event with a stateless map, re-partitions by user id with keyBy, aggregates per-user statistics over thirty-minute tumbling windows, and writes the results to a PostgreSQL sink via JDBC. The design turns on three concepts: parallelism, which is how many parallel subtasks each operator runs; the data-exchange pattern between operators, which is either forwarding when partitioning is preserved or redistributing when a shuffle such as keyBy is required; and fault tolerance, which Flink provides through periodic distributed checkpoints that, combined with a replayable source and an idempotent or transactional sink, give exactly-once end-to-end.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture the National Bank of India tracking parcel-style delivery of physical debit cards to customers. Events about each card's journey stream in through Kafka, already sorted into lanes by customer. A first station stamps each event with extra details, the map enrichment, and because it does not change lanes the parcels flow straight through, forwarding. Then the parcels are re-sorted so that everything for one customer goes to the same clerk, the keyBy shuffle, so each clerk can tally that customer's deliveries over each half hour, the tumbling window. The tallies are filed into the central ledger, the PostgreSQL sink. If the power blips, the bank does not lose count, because it periodically photographs the whole line's progress, the checkpoint, and can rewind the incoming feed to the last photo and continue without double-counting.
s1_definition.oneliner: A Flink delivery-tracking pipeline reads a Kafka source partitioned by user id, forwards through a stateless enrichment map, redistributes via keyBy to aggregate thirty-minute tumbling-window stats per user, and sinks to PostgreSQL, with checkpoints plus a replayable source and idempotent sink giving exactly-once fault tolerance.

**Professional definition:** The pipeline is a Flink streaming job that ingests delivery events from a Kafka source partitioned by user id, enriches each event with a stateless map, re-partitions by user id with keyBy, aggregates per-user statistics over thirty-minute tumbling windows, and writes the results to a PostgreSQL sink via JDBC. The design turns on three concepts: parallelism, which is how many parallel subtasks each operator runs; the data-exchange pattern between operators, which is either forwarding when partitioning is preserved or redistributing when a shuffle such as keyBy is required; and fault tolerance, which Flink provides through periodic distributed checkpoints that, combined with a replayable source and an idempotent or transactional sink, give exactly-once end-to-end.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture the National Bank of India tracking parcel-style delivery of physical debit cards to customers. Events about each card's journey stream in through Kafka, already sorted into lanes by customer. A first station stamps each event with extra details, the map enrichment, and because it does not change lanes the parcels flow straight through, forwarding. Then the parcels are re-sorted so that everything for one customer goes to the same clerk, the keyBy shuffle, so each clerk can tally that customer's deliveries over each half hour, the tumbling window. The tallies are filed into the central ledger, the PostgreSQL sink. If the power blips, the bank does not lose count, because it periodically photographs the whole line's progress, the checkpoint, and can rewind the incoming feed to the last photo and continue without double-counting.

**One line to remember:** A Flink delivery-tracking pipeline reads a Kafka source partitioned by user id, forwards through a stateless enrichment map, redistributes via keyBy to aggregate thirty-minute tumbling-window stats per user, and sinks to PostgreSQL, with checkpoints plus a replayable source and idempotent sink giving exactly-once fault tolerance.

sections.s2_technical:
The source is a Kafka topic partitioned by user id, read by a Flink Kafka source whose parallelism you typically match to the partition count so each subtask owns a share of partitions; for example twelve partitions with source parallelism twelve means one partition per subtask. The source assigns timestamps and watermarks from the event time so downstream windows work correctly. The next operator is a stateless map that enriches each event, for example adding the user's region or the delivery service-level. Because a map does not change how data is partitioned, Flink connects the source to the map with a forwarding exchange, meaning subtask n of the source sends only to subtask n of the map with no network shuffle, which is cheap and keeps data local.

The keyBy is the pivotal step. Aggregating per user requires that all events for a given user reach the same window subtask, but the source's Kafka partitioning, while by user id, does not guarantee alignment with Flink's key groups, so keyBy performs a redistributing exchange: Flink hashes the user id to a key group and routes each record across the network to the subtask responsible for that key group. This shuffle is more expensive than forwarding because it crosses the network, but it is what makes keyed state and per-user windows possible. After the keyBy, a thirty-minute tumbling window groups each user's events into fixed, non-overlapping thirty-minute buckets by event time, and an aggregate function computes the per-user stats, such as the count of delivery events, the number completed, and the average time between scans. The window fires when the watermark passes each window's end, emitting one result row per user per window. Finally a JDBC sink writes those rows to PostgreSQL; you configure batching and set the parallelism of the sink to balance write throughput against database connection limits.

Parallelism is set per operator and governs throughput and resource use. You match source parallelism to partitions, give the keyed window enough parallelism to spread the user keys, and often keep the sink parallelism lower to respect database connection pools. Flink groups chained forwarding operators into tasks for efficiency, so the source and map can run in one task slot, while the shuffle boundary at keyBy separates tasks. Fault tolerance comes from checkpointing: Flink periodically injects barriers into the stream that flow through the dataflow, and when a barrier reaches an operator it snapshots that operator's state, including the Kafka offsets at the source and the open window contents in the keyed window operator, to durable storage such as S3 or HDFS. On failure, Flink restores the last complete checkpoint, resets the Kafka source to the checkpointed offsets, and replays from there; because the window state and offsets are restored together and the sink is idempotent or transactional, no delivery event is counted twice and none is lost. The senior nuances are these. First, align source parallelism with partitions to avoid idle subtasks or uneven load. First-class watermark handling matters because a stalled partition can hold back window firing, so you configure idleness detection. Second, the keyBy shuffle is the main network cost, so you place heavy stateless work before it only if it reduces data volume. Third, choose exactly-once checkpointing with a transactional or upsert JDBC sink for correctness, or at-least-once with idempotent upserts if you can tolerate the simpler mode. Fourth, size checkpoint interval against state size and recovery objectives, and use incremental checkpoints with RocksDB for large window state. Understanding forwarding versus redistributing, matching parallelism to partitions, and how checkpoints plus replayable source and idempotent sink combine for exactly-once is exactly what a scenario interviewer is probing for.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India dispatches physical debit and credit cards to customers and must show each customer a live, accurate count of their card-delivery scan events every half hour, aggregated per customer, which requires routing all of a customer's events to one place and bucketing them by time. This is exactly the keyBy-plus-tumbling-window design.

Problem 2 — The pipeline must never lose or double-count a scan even if a task crashes, because an inaccurate delivery status erodes customer trust. This is exactly what checkpoints plus a replayable Kafka source and an idempotent PostgreSQL upsert sink provide.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that models the whole pipeline's logic without a cluster, emphasizing the exchange patterns and checkpoint recovery. We define a `DeliveryEvent` with a user id, a scan status, and an event time, an `Enricher` representing the forwarding map, a `KeyedWindowAggregator` representing the redistributing keyBy plus thirty-minute tumbling window that computes per-user stats and fires on watermark, and a `CheckpointedRunner` that processes events, periodically checkpoints the window state and source offset, simulates a crash, and replays from the last checkpoint to show exactly-once. A `DeliveryPipelineDemo` main class feeds scan events for two customers across windows, checkpoints, crashes, replays, and prints the per-user window stats and the recovery.

The PostgreSQL sink schema and job config:

```sql
-- create_tables.sql : idempotent upsert target keyed by (user_id, window_start)
CREATE TABLE delivery_stats (
    user_id       VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    window_start  TIMESTAMP   NOT NULL,
    window_end    TIMESTAMP   NOT NULL,
    total_scans   INT         NOT NULL,
    completed     INT         NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, window_start)
);
```

```properties
# job.properties
source.topic=card-delivery-scans
source.partitions=12
source.parallelism=12
window.size.minutes=30
sink.jdbc.url=jdbc:postgresql://db.bank.internal:5432/deliverydb
checkpoint.interval.ms=60000
checkpoint.mode=EXACTLY_ONCE
state.backend=rocksdb
```

sections.s5_journey:
The input is delivery scan events for two customers in the window from zero to thirty minutes, with a checkpoint after three events and a crash before the next checkpoint.

Step 1. The first two scans for SAV2001, picked-up at two minutes and in-transit at ten minutes, enter. The forwarding map enriches each with a region without any shuffle, then keyBy routes both to SAV2001's window bucket, which now counts two scans and zero delivered. The source offset is two.

Step 2. A scan for CUR3001, picked-up at twelve minutes, enters. It is enriched, then keyBy routes it to CUR3001's bucket, which counts one scan. The offset is three.

Step 3. A checkpoint runs. Flink snapshots the window state, SAV2001 with two scans and CUR3001 with one, together with the source offset three, to durable storage. This is the exactly-once anchor.

Step 4. Two more scans arrive: SAV2001 delivered at twenty minutes, offset four, and CUR3001 in-transit at twenty-five minutes, offset five. SAV2001's bucket becomes three scans and one delivered; CUR3001's becomes two scans. These offsets are not yet checkpointed.

Step 5. A crash occurs. On restore, Flink resets the window state to the checkpoint, so SAV2001 is back to two scans and CUR3001 to one, and rewinds the Kafka source to offset three, so it will replay from offset four. Crucially, the uncheckpointed in-flight work at offsets four and five was discarded along with the state, so there is no partial double-count.

Step 6. The source replays offsets four and five, re-delivering the same two scans. They are processed again onto the restored state, bringing SAV2001 back to three scans and one delivered and CUR3001 back to two scans, exactly the same totals as before the crash, counted exactly once. When the watermark passes thirty minutes the window fires, emitting one upsert row per user to PostgreSQL. Because state and offset were restored together and the sink upserts by user and window start, the crash left no trace in the final result.

Final output:

```
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    CHECKPOINT offset=3 windows=2
2024-01-01 00:00:00 WARNING RESTORE offset=3
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    replay from offset 4
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    UPSERT delivery_stats SAV2001@0 total=3 completed=1
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    UPSERT delivery_stats CUR3001@0 total=2 completed=0
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I would design the real-time delivery tracking pipeline as a Flink streaming job with five stages and three design concerns, parallelism, the data-exchange pattern, and fault tolerance. The source is a Kafka topic partitioned by user id, read by a Flink Kafka source whose parallelism I match to the partition count, say twelve subtasks for twelve partitions, with event-time timestamps and watermarks assigned at the source. The second stage is a stateless map that enriches each event, for example adding the customer's region. Because a map does not change the partitioning, Flink connects the source to the map with a forwarding exchange, so subtask n feeds only subtask n with no network shuffle, and the two chain into one task for efficiency. The third stage is keyBy on user id, which is a redistributing exchange: Flink hashes the user id to a key group and shuffles each record over the network to the subtask owning that key group, which is what makes per-user keyed state and windows possible. The fourth stage is a thirty-minute tumbling window that buckets each user's events by event time and aggregates per-user stats, firing when the watermark passes each window's end. The fifth stage is a JDBC sink writing one row per user per window to PostgreSQL, with batching and a parallelism tuned to respect the database connection pool.

The interviewer is really probing forwarding versus redistributing, parallelism matching, and exactly-once. Forwarding is the cheap, local exchange used when partitioning is preserved, as with the enrichment map, while redistributing is the network shuffle used by keyBy to bring all of a key's records together, and it is the main network cost so I keep heavy data-reducing work before it only when it actually shrinks the stream. I match source parallelism to partitions to avoid idle or overloaded subtasks, give the keyed window enough parallelism to spread the user keys, and keep the sink parallelism lower for the database. Fault tolerance comes from checkpointing: Flink injects barriers that flow through the dataflow, and each operator snapshots its state, the Kafka offsets at the source and the open window contents at the window operator, to durable storage. On failure Flink restores the last checkpoint, rewinds the source to the checkpointed offsets, and replays, and because state and offsets are restored together and the JDBC sink upserts idempotently by user and window start, every scan is counted exactly once.

At the National Bank of India this was exactly how we tracked physical card deliveries to customers with a live per-customer half-hourly status. I aligned the source parallelism to the partition count and configured partition-idleness detection so one quiet courier region could not stall the watermark and freeze every customer's window. I placed the enrichment as a forwarding map before the keyBy so it stayed local, accepted the keyBy shuffle as the necessary cost of per-user aggregation, used RocksDB with incremental checkpoints because the window state across many users was large, and chose exactly-once checkpointing with an upsert JDBC sink keyed by user and window start. I could demonstrate recovery concretely: after a simulated crash the window state rewound to the last checkpoint, Kafka replayed the uncheckpointed scans, and the final per-user totals were identical to a no-crash run, with no double-count. Being able to lay out the five stages, explain forwarding versus redistributing and why keyBy shuffles, match parallelism to partitions, and show how checkpoints plus a replayable source and idempotent sink deliver exactly-once is precisely what a scenario interviewer wants to hear.
